patterns.name: Apte II Tarpon Fly
patterns.notes: A Keys-style hackle-and-saddle fly tied in the Stu Apte tradition, distinct from the original Stu Apte Tarpon Fly in its material proportions and hook size; sold commercially by Reel Flies and Jackson Hole Fly Company as a separate pattern.

patterns.name: Millhouse Tarpon Toad
patterns.notes: Andy Mill's tournament-proven version of the Tarpon Toad, tied on a Gamakatsu SL12s and commercially produced by Fulling Mill; favored by Mill — the most decorated Gold Cup Tarpon Tournament winner — for clear-water Keys flats.

patterns.name: Millhouse Tarpon Shrimp
patterns.notes: Andy Mill's shrimp-profile tarpon fly, used as a low-light alternative to his toad pattern, with a larger profile that moves water effectively and excels early in the morning on Keys flats.

patterns.name: Palolo Worm
patterns.notes: A foam-topped subsurface palolo worm imitation tied on a 1/0–2/0 hook in red or rust-orange, designed to match the infamous annual palolo worm hatch on Lower Keys ocean-side flats where tarpon sip worms at the surface.

patterns.name: Gordon Baggett's Stiff Worm
patterns.notes: An epoxy-stiffened palolo worm imitation developed by Capt. Gordon Baggett of Bahia Honda, kept straight in the water on the retrieve to mimic the natural swimming motion of real worms; effective outside hatch periods in clear, bright conditions.

patterns.name: Ruoff's Laid-Up Tarpon Fly
patterns.notes: A natural tan/chartreuse fly with subtle coloration designed for finesse presentations to motionless laid-up tarpon by Keys guide Rick Ruoff, who applied his marine biology background to match the low-contrast tones that appeal to resting fish.

patterns.name: Tarpon Bunny (Black)
patterns.notes: A rabbit-strip tarpon fly developed in the Florida Keys in the 1960s–70s with irresistible underwater action; the black colorway is a go-to dark-water and overcast-day pattern that Norman Duncan and subsequent Keys guides helped establish as a flats staple.

patterns.name: Tarpon Bunny (Tan)
patterns.notes: The natural tan version of the Keys rabbit-strip tarpon fly; popular for clear, bright conditions where a more muted, shrimpy profile outfishes flashier patterns and is considered a Sandy Moret-recommended staple at Florida Keys Outfitters.

patterns.name: Peyote Palolo
patterns.notes: A modern foam palolo worm imitation by Drew Chicone that creates a visible wake and the distinctive near-surface skittering motion of live worms, fished year-round on Keys oceanside flats with a two-handed strip retrieve.

patterns.name: Big Eye Tarpon
patterns.notes: A sparsely tied Keys-style fly by Bob LeMay featuring prominent eyes, palmered hackle, and a light flash accent that creates shrimp-like movement; sold by Umpqua Feather Merchants specifically for the Florida Keys destination.

patterns.name: Peyote Palolo
patterns.notes: Also fished in the Everglades backcountry for juvenile and migratory tarpon; the foam body and two-handed strip retrieve work effectively in mangrove channels where tarpon feed opportunistically on worm-like forage.

patterns.name: Avalon Tarpon Fly
patterns.notes: A Keys-style tarpon pattern developed at the Avalon Fly Fishing Lodge in Cayo Largo by Italian-Cuban guide Mauro Ginevri as a companion to his permit fly, with a slim hackle profile designed for large tarpon in the clear channels of Jardines de la Reina.

patterns.name: Avalon Shrimp
patterns.notes: Mauro Ginevri's landmark shrimp pattern with a beaded monofilament keel that keeps the fly riding hook-up at all speeds; the design specifically addresses Cuban flats where permit feed on outsized shrimp (9 cm+) and has been credited with the Cuban grand slam revolution.

patterns.name: Casa Blanca Crab (Cuban)
patterns.notes: A crab imitation developed at the Casa Blanca lodge area in Cuba, distinct from the Yucatan-origin Casa Blanca Raghead already in the library; tied with local color variations for the turtle-grass and coral-sand flats of Jardines de la Reina.

patterns.name: Cuban Mantis Shrimp
patterns.notes: A mantis-shrimp imitation in Cuban color variations (tan-olive over cream) distinct from the Veverka Mantis Shrimp already in the library; popular among Jardines guides targeting both permit on the flats and large snapper around coral edges.

patterns.name: Jardines Bonefish Fly
patterns.notes: A simple tan-and-pink shrimp imitation tied by Jardines de la Reina guides for the large (3–10 lb) bonefish on the extensive turtle-grass flats; emphasizes a slow-sinking, minimal-disturbance profile for wary Cuban fish in gin-clear water.

patterns.name: Cubera Deceiver
patterns.notes: An oversized baitfish pattern in white-and-chartreuse or black-and-purple tied on 3/0–4/0 hooks, used by Jardines guides on channel edges and drop-offs where giant cubera snapper ambush mullet and mojarra.

patterns.name: Snapper Charlie
patterns.notes: A heavier-hook, weighted-eye variant of the Crazy Charlie style adapted for flats snapper fishing at Jardines de la Reina, tied in pink-and-tan to imitate the small shrimp that mutton snapper tail on shallow grass.

patterns.name: EP Snook Bunny (Cuban)
patterns.notes: A rabbit-strip baitfish pattern in chartreuse-white or black-purple used by Cuban guides in the mangrove channels of Jardines de la Reina for the large snook and juvenile tarpon that concentrate around structure on tidal movements.

regions.name: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)

patterns.name: Platinum Blonde
patterns.originator: Joe Brooks (ca. 1940s, popularized; original credited to Bill Gallasch / Homer Rhode Jr.)
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: An all-white bucktail fly on a silver-tinsel body — the foundational member of the Brooks Blonde series — originally developed for Chesapeake Bay stripers and considered by many the first modern saltwater hi-tie streamer; takes stripers from the Cape to the Outer Banks.

patterns.name: Honey Blonde
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: An all-yellow bucktail Blonde on a gold-tinsel body; one of the most fished color variants in New England for early-morning striper and false albacore blitzes when baitfish show a warm olive-yellow flank.

patterns.name: Strawberry Blonde
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: A red-over-white bucktail Blonde; the color contrast and pulsing bucktail silhouette make it a reliable striper pattern in stained or murky northeast coastal water where high contrast triggers reaction strikes.

patterns.name: Argentine Blonde
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: The original Blonde variant — a light-blue wing over a white tail on a silver-mylar body — developed by Joe Brooks for Chesapeake Bay stripers and Argentine fisheries; works effectively along the Northeast coast as a silhouette baitfish imitation.

patterns.name: Corsair Sand Eel
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: Jack Gartside's realistic sand-eel imitation built from Corsair tubing with a flash-material insert and painted olive lateral line; developed specifically for Martha's Vineyard and Cape Cod flats where sand lance are the dominant baitfish from May through August.

patterns.name: Cape Cod Sand Eel
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: A slim Clouser-Deceiver hybrid on a Mustad 34007 1/0 with white saddle hackles, chartreuse bucktail over white, and a pearl HT Braid body; tied in the heart of sand eel country on Cape Cod and listed as a top-5 go-to striper fly by SaltwaterFlies.com.

patterns.name: Bunker Fly
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: A large synthetic or EP-fiber menhaden imitation (10–14 inches) used along the New Jersey and Massachusetts coasts when adult bunker schools draw trophy stripers to the surface; essential for boat anglers targeting 30–50 lb fish in dense bait situations.

patterns.name: Bunker Spawn Fly
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: A smaller (3–5 inch) juvenile menhaden imitation in white-and-olive or white-and-gray EP fibers, imitating post-spawn peanut bunker in the fall; a critical pattern when juvenile bunker schools concentrate in estuaries and tidal rivers from late summer through October.

patterns.name: Tabory's Sand Eel
patterns.region: Cape Cod & the Striper Coast (MA / RI / CT)
patterns.notes: Lou Tabory's slim, sparse sand-eel imitation — a separate pattern from his Snake Fly — featuring a long, narrow profile and minimal materials that allow it to sink slowly through sand-eel schools off Cape Cod beaches; documented in his book Inshore Fly Fishing as a must-have for summer sand-eel blitzes.

patterns.name: Platinum Blonde
patterns.originator: Joe Brooks (ca. 1940s, popularized; original credited to Bill Gallasch / Homer Rhode Jr.)
patterns.notes: A foundational all-white bucktail streamer used extensively from Moriches Bay to Montauk Point; its hi-tie wing breathes in current and under strip, making it equally effective in the rips and the surf.

patterns.name: Honey Blonde
patterns.notes: The all-yellow Blonde variant is a staple in Long Island Sound during sand eel hatches when the bait shows a warm olive-yellow cast; also effective for false albacore chasing rain bait off Montauk in September.

patterns.name: Corsair Sand Eel
patterns.notes: Described by Jack Gartside as a go-to pattern wherever sand eels are abundant; designed for tandem rigging off Moriches Bay through Montauk where sand lance hold in schools on shallow flats and striper blitzes are predictable.
